What is the TikTok algorithm in 2026?
The TikTok algorithm is the technology that decides what TikTok videos to recommend to each user. It studies what you watch and how you interact, and then suggests videos you’re most likely to enjoy.

No two TikTok users will see the same combination of TikTok videos on their For You Page. This feed is unique and highly personalized. The type of content you see on your FYP will evolve over time, as the algorithm catches on to changes in your interests and viewing preferences.

According to TikTok’s official documentation: “We use recommender systems to offer you a personalized experience. These systems suggest content based on your preferences as expressed through interactions on TikTok, such as following an account or liking a post.”
In short: the For You feed is a personalized recommendation engine, and your job as a marketer is to give it clear signals about who your content is for.

How does the TikTok algorithm work in 2026?

The TikTok algorithm looks at three main signals when ranking content. Of these, engagement signals like watch time and completion rate carry the most weight, and TikTok continuously refines how it weighs the rest.
User interactions: What you watch, like, share, comment on, or skip.
Video information: Captions, hashtags, sounds, effects, and views.
User information: Language, country, device type, and settings.
Likes, shares, comments, watch time, completion rate, “Not Interested” clicks
Captions, hashtags, sounds, effects, trending topics
Device type, language, country, account settings, time zone

Every action you take on TikTok provides the app with information about what kind of content you’re most interested in. Within this category, watch time and completion rate are the strongest signals. If someone watches your video all the way through, or replays it, that tells the algorithm your content is highly engaging.
Here are some of the user interactions that will impact what shows up on your For You feed:
Videos you’ve liked or shared on the app
Videos you’ve added to your favorites
Interests you’ve expressed by interacting with organic content and ads
Creators or sounds you’ve chosen to hide
How long you spend watching a video (and whether you replay it)
Content you create on your own account
Positive signals tell the algorithm to show you more of the same kind of content, while the negative ones will prevent similar content from showing up in your feed.
The TikTok algorithm also collects information about the videos you look for in search and the types of videos you watch in general.

It’s worth noting that TikTok doesn’t just read your metadata. The algorithm can also analyze on-screen text and spoken words to understand what your video is about. This means your voiceover and text overlays are categorization signals too, not just your caption and hashtags.
User information doesn’t have as much influence as user actions or video details, but they still play a role. Some of the user information triggers included in the TikTok algorithm are:
Country setting (you may be more likely to see content from people in your own country, or videos that are particularly popular in your country)
Categories of interest you selected in your new user preferences
These are the settings that help TikTok run smoothly. But, because they’re based on one-time settings, rather than ongoing activity, they aren’t as important to the algorithm.
Does TikTok use a point system?

You may have seen claims that TikTok assigns specific point values to each type of interaction, like 1 point for a like and 5 points for a share. TikTok has not publicly confirmed any such point system.

What we do know is that TikTok uses weighted signals, meaning some interactions matter more than others. Based on TikTok’s documentation and observed behavior, here’s how those signals generally stack up:
Strongest signals: Watch time, completion rate, replays, shares
Strong signals: Comments, follows from the video, saves/favorites
Weaker signals: Device type, language, location
The exact weighting is proprietary and likely changes over time, so focus on creating content that earns the strongest signals rather than trying to game a specific formula.
What’s changed with the TikTok algorithm in 2025 and 2026?

The core ranking signals haven’t changed much, but how TikTok distributes content has. The biggest shifts are around search, video length, and format variety, and each one has a practical implication for how you plan content.

Search signals carry more weight: TikTok has leaned hard into search as a discovery surface, adding features like Search Highlights that surface results directly in the app. Practical takeaway: write captions, voiceovers, and on-screen text with the words people actually type into the search bar.

Longer content gets real distribution: Videos recorded in-app can run up to 10 minutes and uploads up to 60 minutes. The algorithm will push longer videos when completion rates hold up, which means length is no longer a penalty if your content earns the attention.

Carousels and photo mode are no longer an afterthought: TikTok reports that 76% of TikTok users enjoy a mix of images and video on the platform, and image posts now get recommended alongside video in the For You feed.

Community relevance beats broad virality: Distribution increasingly runs through subcultures and interest groups rather than one giant mainstream feed. A video that resonates deeply with #BookTok often outperforms one that’s vaguely interesting to everyone.

Content diversity is built in: TikTok’s recommendation system deliberately breaks up repetitive patterns so users don’t see the same creator or topic over and over. That’s one reason a single video can spike while your next one plateaus, and why consistency matters more than any individual post.
None of this changes the fundamentals. It just means the fastest path to algorithmic distribution in 2026 is content that’s searchable, format-flexible, and clearly made for a specific community.
Content TikTok won’t recommend in 2026 (and why)

Not everything that clears the Community Guidelines is eligible for the For You feed. TikTok maintains a separate list of content types it won’t recommend, even when the post stays live on your profile. Knowing these content restrictions is essential for brand safety, because a single ineligible element can quietly cap your reach.
Here’s what TikTok restricts from recommendation:
Content created by anyone under 16 years old
False or unverified claims about civic and election integrity
Unoriginal content (such as content uploaded with a watermark or a simple GIF)
Promoting tobacco or drugs, or showing excessive alcohol consumption
Live content with the main goal of driving people off-platform.

Content not suitable for young people may be restricted to audiences over 18. And content that violates the Community Guidelines will be removed altogether (and could result in a strike against your account). If you post content that falls into any of these categories, you’ll see that information in TikTok Analytics, where you can also file an appeal.
For enterprise teams, this list is especially important for brand safety. Make sure your content guidelines account for these restrictions so you don’t inadvertently limit your reach.

Connecting with existing communities is more important on TikTok than other social networks. Unlike Facebook, where people mostly engage with friends or accounts they already follow, TikTok’s For You feed is built around fresh content from strangers.

But those strangers can quickly turn into a community. 65% of adult TikTok users say they use the platform to connect with people who share their interests. Additionally, 72% of women on TikTok feel it’s easy to connect and bond with new communities around shared life experiences.
Tap into an existing community and you’ll likely find your content amplified to that audience. Fortunately, TikTok subcultures tend to congregate around hashtags.
Some of the fastest-growing communities on TikTok include:

Understanding your most valuable subcultures can also help you plan your content creation that connects authentically with TikTokers, creating greater credibility, brand loyalty, and even more exposure. TikTok users want brands to take this approach: 76% say they like it when brands are a part of special interest groups on the platform.

2. Hook viewers in the first 3 seconds
TikTok moves fast. This is not the platform to add a wordy intro before you dive into the meat of your video. The hook needs to inspire viewers to stop scrolling.
Watch time tells the TikTok algorithm that this is content worth sharing with other viewers. And the first 3 seconds are where viewers decide to stay or scroll past.
According to TikTok itself, the first three seconds are critical. To grab attention, TikTok suggests:
Starting off with a question that your video will answer
Using a timer or countdown in your title overlay
Flashing ahead to a quick preview of the end result

Hashtags matter for your TikTok strategy, but keywords are just as important. TikTok SEO is critical to teach the algorithm just what your content is about, especially now that 49% of consumers use TikTok as a search engine. And to allow interested TikTokers to find it, of course.
Destination Madison created a TikTok series called Madison’s Iconic Eats, playing off pop-culture themes like set-jetting:

“Social search and TikTok SEO is a huge focus for us,” says Sarah Warner, PR and Communications Manager at Destination Madison. “We want to anticipate what people are looking for and make sure that when they’re looking, they find us first. Doing so gives our content longevity and helps new people find us every day, even when we aren’t posting.”
You could search for trending keywords that match with your content. Or, like Warner, you could use trending topics and keywords to inspire your content.

TikTok captions give you plenty of room to work with. Start looking for trending keywords by region and industry in the TikTok Creative Center. (And if you’re stumped about what to write, try Hootsuite’s free social media caption generator.)
Keep in mind that your caption is not the only place to include keywords. TikTok can also pick them up from your voiceover or text overlay.

You can optimize for TikTok search by using clear keywords in captions, voiceovers, and text overlays. The algorithm relies on these signals to understand your content and match it with people looking for it.

This should be an obvious one, right? Low-quality content is not going to find its way to the For You feed. But just in case you need proof, TikTok’s internal data shows that high-quality content creators get 72% more watch time per video view, and more than 40 times greater follower growth.
And since TikTok is unlike other social platforms, high-quality content is TikTok-first content. In fact, 79% of TikTok users prefer brands that understand content creation specifically for TikTok.
You don’t need any fancy equipment. In fact, TikTok research shows audiences prefer a “less-polished, authentic aesthetic.”

What you do need is decent lighting, a good microphone if you’re going to record audio, and some quick edits and transitions to keep the visuals moving. Here are ways to embrace the TikTok-first aesthetic:

Try different video lengths: Videos recorded in TikTok can be up to 10 minutes long, while uploaded videos can be up to 60 minutes long. TikTok has been increasingly distributing longer content (1 to 3 minutes and beyond), especially when completion rates stay high. If your content holds attention, don’t be afraid to go longer.

Experiment with aspect ratio: Yes, you can now upload horizontal videos to TikTok, and they’ll play in full screen mode on phones. These will also work well with TikTok’s improved desktop interface. We’re not suggesting you abandon vertical videos, but it’s worth testing both formats, especially for different lengths.

Dive into editing: Play around with TikTok’s built-in features like effects and text treatments. According to TikTok: “These native features help keep your content feeling native to the platform which can also help get it on more For You pages!”
Try different formats: 76% of TikTok users say they enjoy a mix of images and video on the platform. Carousels are great too, like this example from @chipotle:

Showcase expertise: Specialized content that highlights unique knowledge and expertise elevates the quality of your TikTok offering and connects to your niche. A couple of suggestions straight from TikTok are to solve a problem, share a hack, or teach something step by step.

Add text to your video: Captions are in general a best practice for accessibility. Text like headlines and intro cards can also help draw viewers in and keep them engaged. And heads-up: More than 30% of TikTokers watch videos on mute and need captions for content. Leave them out and you’re missing out on a third of potential viewers.

High-quality TikTok content is authentic, easy to watch, and made for the platform. Use clear sound, good lighting, captions, and quick edits, and test different lengths and formats to keep people watching.
5. Post consistently and at the right time
Posting at the right time is important for all social media platforms, and that includes TikTok. (That’s why we made this handy cheat sheet of the best times to post on every social platform.)
Engagement is a key signal to the TikTok algorithm, and with roughly half of 18- to 29-year-olds using TikTok at least once a day, posting when your audience is most active is essential.
Hootsuite’s research with Critical Truth shows that overall, the best time to post on TikTok for engagement is either Thursday morning or Saturday midday.

But for best results, you need to know the best time to post for your specific audience. And for best results with the TikTok algorithm, you need to post at the best time to extend reach, which is not always the same as the best time to maximize engagement.

Fortunately, reach is a key goal available in Hootsuite’s Best Time to Publish feature. This handy tool provides custom recommendations based on your past performance and tailored to your unique audience and their activity patterns on TikTok.

Consistency matters just as much as timing. Posting regularly signals to the algorithm that your account is active and worth distributing, so maintaining a regular cadence is important for algorithmic momentum.
6. Boost reach with duets, stitches, and LIVE

Duets and Stitches are two of the easiest ways to borrow distribution from content that’s already working. When you Duet or Stitch a video, your post generates engagement signals of its own while staying linked to the original, which puts you in front of an audience that has already shown interest in that topic.
A few ways to use them well:
React to a community conversation: Duet a creator in your niche with a genuine take, not a generic “so true.”
Answer a question: Stitch a video that poses a problem your brand can actually solve.
Build a chain: Invite your audience to Duet your video, which multiplies interactions across many accounts.

TikTok LIVE works differently but serves the same goal. Live sessions appear in a dedicated discovery surface and generate sustained watch time, comments, and follows in a short window. Keep the format simple: a Q&A, a behind-the-scenes look, or a product walkthrough is enough. Just remember that Duets and Stitches are only available when the original creator enables them, and your own settings control whether others can do the same to your videos. If you’re scheduling TikToks through Hootsuite, you can toggle Duet and Stitch permissions directly from the Composer.
Hashtags are still a categorization signal. They tell the algorithm which community hashtags and topics your video belongs to, which helps TikTok find the right first audience to test it on.
The approach that works best in 2026 is a mix:
Broad community tags: One or two established subculture tags like #BookTok or #STEMTok to signal the neighborhood your content lives in.
Niche descriptive tags: Two or three specific tags that describe exactly what the video covers, so you compete in a smaller, more relevant pool.
Branded or campaign tags: One tag you can track over time for reporting.

What doesn’t work is stuffing 20 unrelated hashtags into a caption and hoping something sticks. Since TikTok’s search function now reads captions, voiceovers, and on-screen text, hashtags alone carry less weight than they used to. Pair a short, focused hashtag set with keyword-rich copy and you cover both discovery paths at once.

Trending sounds function a lot like hashtags. They group your video with every other post using that audio, which gives the algorithm another clear signal about where your content fits and who might want to see it.

Timing is the part most brands get wrong. A sound is most useful early in its lifecycle, while usage is climbing and the pool of competing videos is still small. By the time a sound is everywhere, the discovery advantage is mostly gone. The Trends section of TikTok Creative Center is a good place to spot sounds on the way up rather than on the way out.

One important caveat for brands: business accounts can only use audio from TikTok’s Commercial Music Library, which is pre-cleared for commercial use. Popular chart music is generally off-limits for business accounts, and using unlicensed audio can get your video muted or taken down. Build your sound strategy around the Commercial Music Library, original audio, and your own voiceovers.
9. Track your performance with TikTok analytics

You can’t optimize for the algorithm without seeing which signals your content is actually earning. TikTok’s native analytics, available in any business or creator account, map directly to the ranking signals that matter.
Average watch time: The clearest proxy for how well your hook and pacing are working.
Completion rate: The strongest indicator that the algorithm will keep pushing a video.
Traffic source types: Shows whether views came from the For You feed, search, your profile, or your followers. A rising share of search traffic means your TikTok SEO is landing.
Retention graph: Pinpoints the exact second viewers drop off, which tells you what to cut next time.

10. Work with TikTok creators and influencers

Creator partnerships give you something you can’t manufacture on your own account: an audience that already trusts the person delivering your message. That trust shows up as stronger engagement signals, and strong engagement signals are what drive distribution.

The algorithm doesn’t give creator content special treatment. What it does reward is the engagement that good creator content tends to generate, because a creator knows the cadence, humor, and format their community responds to.

TikTok Creator Marketplace is the official place to find partners, filter by audience demographics and engagement rate, and manage campaigns. When you’re evaluating creators, look past follower count at average views per video, comment quality, and how closely their audience overlaps with the community you’re targeting.

A creator with 20,000 highly engaged niche followers will often outperform one with 500,000 passive ones. And give them creative latitude. Scripts that sound like ad copy are the fastest way to undermine the authenticity that made the partnership worth doing.

TikTok Shop content is eligible for recommendation in the For You feed as well as the Shop tab, which means product videos and live shopping sessions can earn organic distribution the same way any other post does. TikTok continues to invest heavily in commerce features, projected to reach 57.7 million U.S. buyers in 2026, and that investment signals ongoing algorithmic support for shoppable content.
The catch is that shoppable content still has to earn watch time. A straight product demo with no hook performs exactly as poorly as any other low-engagement video, tagged or not.
Lead with the use case: Show the problem your product solves in the first few seconds, then tag it.
Use live shopping for depth: LIVE sessions let you answer real questions and generate sustained watch time in one sitting.
Let creators do the selling: Affiliate partnerships put your product in front of established communities with built-in credibility.
Treat TikTok Shop as one format in your content mix rather than a separate channel, and the algorithm will treat it the same way it treats everything else you post.
This sounds soft, but it’s the most practical advice on the list. The algorithm rewards content that holds attention, and nothing holds attention like a real person being genuinely interesting.

TikTok’s own research on the less-polished aesthetic points the same direction: audiences would rather watch something honest than something perfect. Hootsuite’s Social Media Trends research confirms the same pattern across platforms, with authenticity consistently outperforming polish.

So let your team’s personality show. Try formats that feel slightly outside your brand comfort zone. Reply to comments with video. The accounts that grow consistently on TikTok are usually the ones that look like they’re enjoying themselves, and that enjoyment is exactly what keeps people watching to the end.
How to tell if the TikTok algorithm is working for you

The clearest sign the algorithm is distributing your content is that most of your views come from people who don’t follow you. Follower counts and likes feel good, but they don’t tell you much about distribution on their own.
Here’s what to monitor, and what each metric actually reveals:
For You feed traffic share: If a high percentage of views come from the For You feed, the algorithm is actively recommending you. A low percentage means you’re mostly reaching existing followers.
Average watch time and completion rate: Rising numbers here usually come before rising reach, because these are the signals that trigger wider distribution.
Search traffic share: Growing search views mean your keyword work is compounding and your older content is still earning views.
Shares and saves: Both signal that a video was worth passing on, which is a stronger vote of confidence than a like.
Follower growth rate: Measured as new followers per 1,000 views, this tells you whether new reach is converting into audience.

Look at these as trends across 30 to 90 days, not single posts. Because TikTok deliberately varies what it recommends, one video can spike while the next flattens, and that variance says more about the platform than about your strategy.

If you’re reporting up to leadership, pulling these numbers manually every month gets old fast. How often does the TikTok algorithm change?

The TikTok algorithm changes incrementally and continuously, though TikTok doesn’t announce every update. The core ranking signals (watch time, completion rate, user interactions) stay consistent, but how TikTok weighs certain content types and discovery surfaces evolves as user behavior shifts. Monitor your performance metrics regularly and stay informed through TikTok’s official documentation and Creator Academy so you can adapt.
Does posting frequency affect the TikTok algorithm?

Yes, posting frequency does affect the TikTok algorithm, but consistency matters more than volume. The algorithm favors active accounts that post regularly, since this signals your content is current and your account is worth distributing. Posting low-quality content to hit a quota can hurt performance, so aim for a sustainable cadence you can maintain without compromising quality.
Can you reset the TikTok algorithm?

You cannot fully reset the TikTok algorithm, but you can influence what it shows you by changing your viewing behavior. To refresh your For You feed, watch and engage with the types of content you want more of, and use the “Not Interested” button on content you want to avoid. For brands, if your content isn’t performing, focus on improving quality and relevance rather than trying to game the system. The algorithm responds to genuine engagement signals.
How important are hashtags for the TikTok algorithm in 2026?

Hashtags remain important for the TikTok algorithm in 2026, but their role has evolved alongside TikTok’s expanded search functionality. Hashtags help categorize your content and connect it to specific communities, while keyword-optimized captions, voiceovers, and on-screen text now carry equal or greater weight for discoverability. Use a mix of broad community hashtags and specific niche tags, and pair them with natural language people actually search for.
What metrics should enterprise teams track to measure TikTok algorithm performance?

Enterprise teams should track watch time, completion rate, shares, and saves as primary indicators of algorithmic performance, since these are the strongest ranking signals. Also monitor reach, profile views, traffic source types, and follower growth rate. Use TikTok’s native analytics to identify which content the algorithm favors, and track performance by content type, community, and keyword. Tools like Hootsuite can centralize this data and surface patterns across your content portfolio.
What is the 3-second rule on TikTok?

The 3-second rule on TikTok refers to the critical first three seconds of a video, which is the window where viewers decide to keep watching or scroll past. Because watch time is the strongest ranking signal, losing people in those three seconds caps how far the algorithm will distribute your video. TikTok recommends opening with a question, a countdown or timer overlay, or a quick preview of the end result.
Is 20,000 views on TikTok considered viral?

Whether 20,000 views counts as viral depends on your account size and niche, but for most creators and brands, 20,000 views signals strong algorithmic distribution beyond your existing followers. A more useful benchmark than raw view count is the ratio of views to followers, plus how much of that traffic came from the For You feed. If most views came from people who don’t follow you, the algorithm is working in your favor.
How do you trigger the TikTok algorithm?

You trigger the TikTok algorithm by creating content that earns strong engagement signals, especially high watch time, completion rate, shares, and comments, in the first hours after posting. Practically, that means hooking viewers in the first three seconds, keeping the video tight enough that people finish it, posting when your audience is active, and giving the algorithm clear topic signals through keywords, hashtags, and sounds.
Does the TikTok algorithm favor longer videos in 2026?

The TikTok algorithm does not automatically favor longer videos, but it increasingly distributes longer content of one to three minutes and beyond when completion rates and engagement remain high. Length is neutral. What matters is whether people watch to the end. Test longer formats for topics that genuinely need the time, and watch your retention graph to see where attention drops.
How does TikTok’s search algorithm differ from the For You feed algorithm?

TikTok’s search algorithm prioritizes keyword relevance in captions, voiceovers, and on-screen text, while the For You feed algorithm weighs engagement signals like watch time and interactions more heavily. The practical implication is that search rewards clarity and specificity, so content optimized for search keeps earning views long after it stops appearing in the feed. Optimizing for both gives your content two discovery paths instead of one.
